speaker: Peter Beck
title: How Rocket Lab CEO Sir Peter Beck Is Building a Multi-Generational Space Company
question: In aerospace and defense manufacturing, how does owning critical subsystem suppliers change the economics of competing for major prime contracts?
guest: We play in areas where we think we can be disruptive and add real value over others. National security is one of those areas that has typically been pretty underserved. The typical national security contract would go to the typical primes, cost-plus, blow out in time and blow out in money. We are just not built like that. When we go into the national security world, it is firm fixed price and we deliver, which is a different paradigm for some of these customers. Even when we go after those big prime contracts—we are prime on two national security programs right now—even if we lose, we still win, and when we win, we win twice. We will go head-to-head with a prime for a contract, and if we lose, the next day there is a whole bunch of purchase orders for reaction wheels, solar, and other components. When we win alongside other primes, we win twice. Our SDA contract was a great example: we won an $800 million contract and two other primes also won contracts, which turned into over a billion-dollar contract for us because those primes needed our stuff.

points.core: Losing a prime bid still generates revenue selling critical components to winners.
points.note: Accept: defeated prime bidders supplying subsystems like reaction wheels or solar panels to the winning contractor. Do not credit: generic claims about diversifying revenue streams or vertical integration lowering costs.

points.core: Multi-award prime contracts generate extra upside by supplying components to rival winners.
points.note: Accept: capturing both a direct prime award and subcontracted hardware orders from co-winning primes on split awards. Do not credit: vague mentions of winning bigger contracts or cross-selling.

points.core: Firm-fixed-price execution differentiates challengers from legacy cost-plus primes prone to overruns.
points.note: Accept: fixed-price contracting avoiding traditional cost-plus schedule or budget blowouts in defense procurement. Do not credit: generic praise for being faster or cheaper without contrasting contract structures.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Owning a critical subsystem supplier shifts a prime's position in three ways: cost, control, and leverage over rivals.

On cost, the integrated prime captures the supplier's margin instead of paying it, so it can bid more aggressively or earn more at the same price. It also gains better visibility into true subsystem costs and more control over schedule and supply risk, which matters in fixed-price development bids where overruns come out of the contractor's pocket.

On leverage, if the subsystem has few alternative sources (solid rocket motors, for example), competing primes must buy from a rival's subsidiary. That creates the potential to raise rivals' costs, deprioritize their orders, or gain insight into their designs and pricing. Boeing declined to bid on the ICBM replacement (GBSD/Sentinel) after Northrop Grumman acquired Orbital ATK, citing that motor advantage.

The offsetting factor is regulators. The FTC imposed firewall and non-discrimination conditions on Northrop–Orbital ATK and blocked Lockheed Martin's acquisition of Aerojet Rocketdyne in 2022; L3Harris later bought Aerojet as a non-prime "merchant supplier." Integration also carries capital burden and can dull the acquired supplier's sales to other primes.

points.why: The response describes rivals buying from the integrated supplier but does not connect those sales to revenue after the supplier’s parent loses a prime bid.
The response does not describe earning both a direct prime award and subsystem revenue from other winners on the same procurement.
The response notes that fixed-price overruns come out of the contractor’s pocket but does not contrast fixed-price execution with legacy cost-plus contracting and its overruns.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Owning critical subsystem suppliers—such as propulsion, sensors, or avionics—fundamentally reshapes prime contract competition by eliminating margin stacking and shifting how profits are captured across a program’s lifecycle. An integrated prime avoids paying a subcontractor’s markup ("fee-on-fee"), allowing it to submit more aggressive bids on initial development awards while preserving consolidated margins, or to accept thinner platform margins in exchange for lucrative, decades-long subsystem sustainment, spares, and upgrade revenues.

Vertical ownership also reduces hold-up and schedule risk by aligning R&D investment, cost visibility, and intellectual property control internally. Simultaneously, controlling bottleneck inputs alters rivals’ economics: even when regulators impose firewalls and non-discriminatory supply mandates, competing primes face slower co-design and reluctance to share sensitive architectures with a competitor’s subsidiary—while the integrated owner still collects merchant-supplier margins even if a rival wins the prime award. The primary trade-off is higher fixed overhead and capital intensity, forcing the prime to sustain enough internal and external volume to keep specialized manufacturing assets utilized and avoid locking itself into legacy in-house technology.

points.why: The candidate explicitly says the integrated bidder still profits from subsystem sales when a rival wins the prime award.
quotes: the integrated owner still collects merchant-supplier margins even if a rival wins the prime award

points.why: The candidate never describes earning subsystem revenue from co-winning primes while also holding a direct award on the same program.
The candidate attributes lower schedule risk to vertical ownership and omits the contrast between firm-fixed-price and cost-plus contracting.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Owning critical subsystem suppliers changes the economics of a prime contract bid in four main ways.

**Margin capture and pricing.** A vertically integrated prime keeps the profit that would otherwise go to subcontractors. It can price a bid aggressively and still make money at the component level, though this is partly limited. Under FAR 31.205‑26(e), parts transferred between divisions of the same company on cost‑type work are usually charged at cost, with no added profit, unless commercial or competitive pricing applies.

**Cost and schedule control.** Control of scarce items like solid rocket motors, seekers or radars gives the prime more confidence in its cost and delivery estimates. That lowers the risk premium it needs in fixed‑price or incentive bids, and it lets the prime design the system around its own subsystems.

**Leverage over rivals.** When competitors need the same supplier, the owner can learn their plans, delay them or raise their costs. That's why regulators step in. The FTC let Northrop buy Orbital ATK in 2018 (now part of Northrop) only with firewalls and fair‑supply rules for missile motors. In 2022 it effectively blocked Lockheed's purchase of Aerojet Rocketdyne, which L3Harris later bought.

**The tradeoff.** Integration ties up capital and can drive away outside customers, and the government may discount its value or impose conditions.

points.why: The response discusses supplier leverage over rivals but never explains how a losing bidder earns component revenue from the winner.
The response does not describe winning a prime award and also selling hardware to other primes that win awards on the same program.
The response links subsystem control to lower fixed-price bid risk but does not contrast firm-fixed-price execution with schedule or budget overruns under legacy cost-plus contracts.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Owning critical subsystem suppliers—such as propulsion, avionics, or sensor manufacturers—reshapes prime-contract competition through both cost and strategic leverage. First, vertical integration eliminates double marginalization: the prime captures the subsystem supplier's profit margin internally, allowing it to submit more competitive bids or earn higher margins across a program's lifecycle. Direct ownership also improves schedule reliability, supply-chain security, and early co-engineering, which are heavily weighted in defense source selections.

Second, controlling a bottleneck component creates asymmetric competitive power. A vertically integrated prime can raise rivals' costs, prioritize its own integration schedules, or gain insight into competitors' technical proposals—dynamics that frequently trigger antitrust scrutiny and mandatory information firewalls. Even when an integrated prime loses a major award, owning the underlying subsystem lets it hedge its risk by capturing a lucrative share of the winner's program as a merchant supplier.

The main trade-off is capital intensity and market friction: competing primes may actively qualify alternative suppliers to avoid funding a rival, potentially shrinking the captive supplier's external revenue base if internal prime wins do not offset lost third-party sales.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Owning a critical subsystem supplier lets an aerospace or defense prime earn profit on both the subsystem and the finished platform. On a competitive fixed-price bid, it can pass some of that savings to the customer by pricing the subsystem below what an independent supplier would charge, while still preserving its overall margin. Control over subsystem design and production can also reduce integration costs and give the prime more confidence in its delivery schedule. If the subsidiary sells to rival bidders, the parent can earn revenue on the winning program even when it loses the prime contract.

The trade-off is that the prime takes on the supplier’s fixed costs, capital investment, and production risk. The economics are strongest when the subsystem is hard to replace and has enough demand across programs to keep capacity utilized. Rival primes may seek alternative suppliers, and government cost and competition rules can limit how the owner prices internal transfers or restricts access.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Owning a critical subsystem supplier gives a prime contractor more room to price its bid. It can accept a lower margin on the subsystem to make the overall offer more competitive, weighing the profit on the whole contract. Control over design and delivery can also reduce integration costs and schedule risk, making the bid more credible.

If rival primes need the same subsystem, the owner may still earn supplier profit even when it loses the prime contract. That cushions the loss, but it also changes how much a win is worth. If the owner would supply the subsystem either way, only the additional profit from winning justifies a deeper bid discount. Ownership pays off when those profits and cost savings outweigh the acquisition price, the fixed cost of maintaining the supplier, and any sales lost as rivals seek alternatives.
